title: 22. Interview: Availability
summary: Interview Q&A for Availability — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Availability interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Explain the "9s table" and why the jump from four nines to five is so expensive.
**Answer:** The 9s table maps an availability percentage to its allowed downtime per year: 99% allows 3.65 days, 99.9% allows 8.76 hours, 99.99% allows 52.6 minutes, 99.999% allows 5.26 minutes. Each additional nine cuts the budget by 10x. The jump from three to four nines is achievable with redundancy and automated failover — multiple instances, read replicas, multi-AZ deployment. The jump from four to five nines is qualitatively different. With a 5-minute annual budget, you cannot afford a single manual failover (which takes 5–30 minutes), so failover must be fully automated and tested regularly. You cannot afford planned maintenance, so deploys must be zero-downtime rolling or blue-green, and schema migrations must be online expand-contract. You cannot afford a single bad deploy, so you need canaries and automated rollbacks. You cannot afford a single region incident, so you need multi-region active-active. Each of these is expensive in engineering and operations, and the marginal cost rises steeply. Five nines is roughly 5–10x the cost of four nines for most workloads.

**Visual:**
```
9s    allowed downtime / year
2     3.65 days         <- single server, manual ops
3     8.76 hours        <- LB + replicas + multi-AZ
4     52.6 minutes      <- multi-AZ + automated failover
5     5.26 minutes      <- multi-region active-active + chaos eng + zero-downtime deploys
```

### Q2. Define MTBF and MTTR, and explain why modern systems focus on MTTR more than MTBF.
**Answer:** MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) is the average time the system runs correctly before failing; MTTR (Mean Time To Recover) is the average time from failure to full recovery. Availability equals `MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)`, so you can raise availability by raising MTBF (fewer failures) or lowering MTTR (faster recovery). Modern distributed systems focus on MTTR because raising MTBF is increasingly hard. Every component fails — disks die, networks partition, instances disappear, humans push bad config. The number of failure modes grows super-linearly with the number of components, so for any sufficiently large system, failures are guaranteed and frequent. The realistic strategy is to accept that failures will happen and engineer for fast recovery: automated health checks that detect failures in seconds, blue-green deploys that allow rollback in under a minute, self-healing autoscalers that replace unhealthy instances, runbooks that an on-call can execute in minutes, and chaos engineering that tests the recovery paths before a real incident does. A system that fails weekly but recovers in 30 seconds has higher availability than one that fails yearly but takes 4 hours to recover.

**Visual:**
```
A = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)

Strategy A (raise MTBF):  fewer failures, but capped by reality of distributed systems
Strategy B (lower MTTR):  failures still happen, but recovery in seconds
                          -> modern focus: chaos eng, auto-rollback, self-heal

Example:
  rare+slow:  MTBF=30d, MTTR=2h  -> 99.72%  (3 nines -1)
  often+fast: MTBF=2d,  MTTR=30s -> 99.98%  (nearly 4 nines)
```

### Q3. What is the difference between planned and unplanned downtime, and why does it matter for the availability budget?
**Answer:** Unplanned downtime is the result of a failure — a crash, a network outage, a bad deploy that escapes canary. Planned downtime is intentional — a maintenance window for upgrades, a schema migration, a hardware refresh. Many teams treat planned downtime as "free" because it is scheduled and announced, but it is not free in availability terms: a 4-hour quarterly maintenance window alone consumes 16 hours per year, exceeding the entire 52-minute budget for four nines. Mature systems eliminate planned downtime via deployment patterns. Rolling deploys replace instances one at a time behind a load balancer, so the service never goes down. Blue-green deploys run two full environments and switch traffic atomically. Canary deploys route a small fraction of traffic to the new version, monitor, and ramp up. Online schema migrations use the expand-contract pattern (add column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, drop old column) so the database is never offline. The discipline is: if a change requires downtime, the change is wrong; redesign the change. A system that has eliminated planned downtime can hit four or five nines; one that has not is capped at three.

**Visual:**
```
Planned downtime (counts against budget!):
   quarterly 4h maintenance windows = 16 h/year  >  52 min budget for 4-nines

Eliminate via:
   rolling deploy      : replace instances one-by-one behind LB
   blue-green          : switch traffic atomically between two envs
   canary              : small % of traffic -> monitor -> ramp
   expand-contract     : add col -> dual-write -> backfill -> switch -> drop
```

### Q4. What is a single point of failure (SPOF), and how do you eliminate one at each tier?
**Answer:** A SPOF is a component whose failure takes down the whole system, regardless of redundancy elsewhere. A classic SPOF is a single load balancer — even if you have 100 web instances behind it, if the LB dies, the service dies. Eliminating SPOFs is tier-by-tier work. At the load-balancer tier: run LBs in active-active pairs or behind anycast DNS (Cloudflare, Route53). At the compute tier: run N instances across multiple AZs behind the LB. At the cache tier: run Redis in primary-replica with Sentinel or Cluster mode, or use DynamoDB which is inherently multi-AZ. At the database tier: run a primary with synchronous replicas in another AZ, with automated failover (RDS Multi-AZ, Aurora). At the network tier: use multiple ISPs or a CDN that absorbs traffic regionally. At the DNS tier: use multiple DNS providers (Route53 + Cloudflare). The discipline is to draw the architecture, walk every component, and ask "if this one thing dies, does the system stay up?" If the answer is no, add redundancy or accept the risk explicitly. Unspoken SPOFs — a single cloud account, a single TLS certificate, a single on-call engineer — are the most dangerous because no one is looking at them.

**Visual:**
```
Per-tier SPOF elimination:

  DNS        : Route53 + Cloudflare (multi-provider)
  LB         : active-active pair, anycast
  Compute    : N instances across 3 AZs
  Cache      : Redis primary-replica + Sentinel, or DynamoDB
  Database   : primary + sync replica in another AZ, auto-failover
  Network    : multi-ISP, CDN absorbing regional traffic
```

### Q5. Explain the 2017 AWS S3 us-east-1 outage and the system-design lessons.
**Answer:** In February 2017, an engineer running a debugging playbook executed a command with a typo that exceeded its intended scope, removing a larger-than-intended set of capacity from the S3 index subsystem in us-east-1. The index service was designed to handle individual node failures gracefully, but the simultaneous removal of many nodes triggered a metadata re-rebalancing storm that took the index service down for roughly four hours. Because S3 is a foundational dependency — thousands of services use it for assets, configuration, Lambda code, backups — the blast radius was enormous, affecting a large fraction of the internet. The system-design lessons: (1) **operational tooling must isolate blast radius** — a command that can take down a subsystem should require explicit confirmation and should be scoped mechanically, not by human accuracy; (2) **dependency concentration amplifies failures** — when every service depends on one S3 bucket, one incident has massive blast radius, so critical dependencies should be isolated or sharded; (3) **MTTR dominated the availability impact** — the system was designed for failure, but recovery required the re-rebalancing to complete, which took hours; (4) **single-region is a real risk** — customers with cross-region replication or multi-region active-active architectures survived, while single-region customers did not. The post-incident changes included tooling changes, index-subsystem re-architecture, and stronger cross-region failover tooling.

**Visual:**
```
Engineer typo -> command exceeds scope -> many S3 index nodes removed
   -> metadata rebalancing storm -> S3 index down ~4h in us-east-1
   -> thousands of dependent services down (S3 is foundational)
Lessons:
   - tooling must mechanically scope destructive commands
   - dependency concentration amplifies blast radius
   - MTTR dominated (rebalancing had to finish)
   - cross-region replication saved customers who had it
```

### Q6. Why does Netflix run multi-region active-active, and how do they verify it works?
**Answer:** Netflix targets 99.99% availability (52 minutes per year). A single AWS region cannot meet that budget — AWS regions occasionally have multi-hour incidents, and a single region's incidents alone would consume the entire annual budget. Multi-region active-active is the architectural response: both US-East and US-West serve live traffic at full capacity, data is replicated asynchronously between regions, and either can carry the entire load if the other fails. Failover does not require provisioning new capacity — the surviving region is already running — so traffic shifts in minutes via DNS. The reason Netflix invests so heavily in chaos engineering (the Simian Army) is to verify that the active-active design actually fails over when needed. Chaos Monkey kills random instances in production to verify instance-level redundancy. Latency Monkey injects network latency to verify timeout and retry logic. The regional Failover Monkey periodically shifts all traffic to one region to verify the failover path works end-to-end. The principle: an availability design that has never been tested in production is a hypothesis, not a design; you must routinely exercise the failure modes you claim to handle, or you will discover they do not work during a real incident.

**Visual:**
```
        Geo-DNS
        /     \
   [US-East]  [US-West]   both active, both at full capacity
      |           |
   Cassandra  <-> Cassandra   async replication
      |           |
   [each region can carry 100% of traffic if the other dies]

Verification: Simian Army
   Chaos Monkey  : kills instances
   Latency Monkey: injects latency
   Failover Monkey: shifts all traffic to one region (regularly, in prod)
```

### Q7. What is a cascading failure, and how do you prevent it?
**Answer:** A cascading failure is when a failure in one component triggers failures in its callers, which trigger failures in their callers, radiating outward until a large fraction of the system is down. The classic mechanism: service B becomes slow; service A's calls to B start timing out, but A holds its connection pool waiting for those timeouts; A's connection pool exhausts, so A cannot accept new requests even for paths that do not depend on B; A becomes slow to its callers; the pattern repeats. Prevention techniques: (1) **timeouts everywhere** — never let a call wait indefinitely; pick a timeout shorter than the connection pool's patience; (2) **circuit breakers** — when failures to B exceed a threshold, stop calling B for a cool-down period (Hystrix, Resilience4j, Envoy); (3) **bulkheads** — separate connection pools per downstream so a slow B does not exhaust the pool that serves C; (4) **backpressure** — when a queue grows past a threshold, reject new work with 429/503 rather than letting latency grow unbounded; (5) **graceful degradation** — return a partial or cached response rather than failing the whole request when a non-critical dependency is unavailable. The architectural lesson: every downstream call is a potential failure propagator, and the system must be designed to contain failures, not amplify them.

**Visual:**
```
Without protection (cascade):
   B slow -> A times out -> A's pool exhausts -> A slow -> callers of A slow -> ...

With protection:
   B slow -> A's circuit breaker opens (no calls to B for 30s)
          -> A returns degraded/cached response (still serves other paths)
          -> bulkhead: pool for B isolated from pool for C
          -> backpressure: A returns 429 if its own queue > threshold
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your service has a 99.99% availability target but ran for 6 months with zero downtime. Is that good news?
**Answer:** It is concerning, not purely good news. A 99.99% target allows 52 minutes of downtime per year — roughly 26 minutes per six months. Six months with zero downtime could mean the system is genuinely more available than the target, but it more likely means the failure modes that would consume the budget have not occurred yet, or have not been detected. Two specific concerns: (1) **untested failure paths** — if the system has never failed over to its replica, the failover mechanism has never been exercised in production; when a real incident occurs, the failover may not work, and the resulting MTTR could blow the entire annual budget in one event. (2) **silent failures** — the service may be returning 200s but with stale data, partial outages, or elevated error rates that the availability probe does not catch. The right response is to deliberately test the failure paths via chaos engineering: kill instances, inject latency, failover to the replica, simulate a region loss — in a controlled way, during business hours, with the team watching. A system that has survived chaos exercises has demonstrable availability; a system that has merely been lucky does not. Six months of luck is not a design.

**Visual:**
```
6 months, 0 downtime -> lucky, OR untested failure paths

Proactive verification (chaos eng):
   - kill an instance       -> does the LB reroute?
   - kill the primary       -> does failover work? how long?
   - inject 200ms latency   -> do timeouts trip? circuit breakers?
   - failover to other region -> does DNS switch? data consistent?

Better: small controlled failures now than one big uncontrolled one later.
```

### Q2. Your API's availability probe shows 100% uptime, but users complain it is "broken." Diagnose.
**Answer:** The probe is measuring the wrong thing. Availability probes typically check `GET /health` returning 200, which only verifies the process is up — not that it can serve real requests. Users complaining means the service is failing in ways the probe does not capture: (1) **partial dependency failure** — the API is up but the database is slow, so every real request times out while `/health` still returns 200; (2) **stale data** — reads return cached data from yesterday, technically 200 but functionally wrong; (3) **elevated error rate on specific paths** — `/health` works but `/checkout` returns 500s for 30% of requests; (4) **regional issue** — the probe runs from one region and gets 200, but users in another region get timeouts; (5) **mobile client breakage** — the server is fine, but a new app version broke the client. The fix is multi-dimensional monitoring: probe real user paths (synthetic transactions that hit `/search` and `/checkout`), measure error rates and latency per endpoint, monitor from multiple regions, collect client-side telemetry (RUM) so you see what users actually experience, and define availability as "successful real requests / total real requests," not "health endpoint returned 200." A health-check endpoint that always returns 200 is a lie the system tells itself.

**Visual:**
```
Old probe:   GET /health -> 200  (process is alive)
                          BUT users say "broken"

Real availability:
   synthetic:  GET /search -> 200, latency 250ms  (was 50ms)
   error rate: /checkout  -> 30% 500s
   RUM:        p99 from mobile in EU -> 8s
   region:     probe in US-East is fine; EU users timeout

Fix: measure successful real requests / total real requests, per endpoint, per region
```

### Q3. You are designing a payments service targeting 99.99% availability. The CFO refuses to fund multi-region. What do you do?
**Answer:** I would treat this as a misalignment between the NFR and the budget, and force a resolution rather than silently accepting the risk. The math: a single AWS region has had multi-hour incidents (the 2017 S3 outage was ~4 hours in us-east-1), and a single region's annual incident budget alone exceeds the 52-minute target for 99.99%. So if multi-region is not funded, 99.99% is not achievable — the target must change or the budget must change. I would present three explicit options: (1) keep 99.99% target, fund multi-region — the engineering work is ~6 months and ongoing ops cost is roughly 2x single-region; (2) lower the target to 99.9% (8.7 hours/year), stay single-region, and accept that a major region incident will cause an outage of several hours; (3) keep 99.99% but define it as "per-region" — each region meets 99.99% on its own traffic, but a region-level incident causes an outage for that region's users only. For payments specifically, I would also argue that integrity (no double-charge, no lost txn) is the more important NFR, and that a single-region system with strong idempotency, durable event sourcing, and reconciliation jobs may be acceptable even at 99.9% availability. The point is to make the trade-off explicit, not to absorb it silently.

**Visual:**
```
CFO says: no multi-region funding
   |
   +--> Option 1: keep 99.99%, fund multi-region (~6mo, 2x ops cost)
   +--> Option 2: lower to 99.9% (8.7h/yr), stay single-region, accept outages
   +--> Option 3: 99.99% per-region, region incident = region-only outage
   +--> For payments: emphasize INTEGRITY (idempotency, event sourcing, reconcile)
```

### Q4. A bad deploy caused a 30-minute outage. Your availability target is 99.99% (52 min/year). How do you respond?
**Answer:** First, this single incident has consumed over half the annual budget — it is a serious event, not a minor hiccup. The response has two phases. **Recovery**: roll back immediately, verify recovery, and communicate. Do not try to fix-forward under pressure — rollback is the safe move. **Post-incident**: treat this as a process failure, not just a code failure. The questions to ask: why did the bad deploy escape canary? Was there a canary at all, or was it a direct push? Were the right metrics monitored during canary, or did the deploy "look green" because the wrong signals were watched? Was the rollback automated (target: under 60 seconds) or manual (target: under 5 minutes), and did it actually meet that target? The architectural action items: (1) require canary deploys for all services, with automated rollback on error-rate or latency thresholds; (2) invest in deploy-time observability so canary decisions are based on real metrics, not "looks fine"; (3) practice rollbacks regularly so the muscle memory exists; (4) add pre-deploy automated checks (unit tests, integration tests, schema migrations) to catch the class of bug before it reaches canary. The deeper lesson: at 99.99%, you cannot afford more than one bad-deploy outage per year — the deploy process itself must be a high-availability subsystem.

**Visual:**
```
30-min outage = 58% of 52-min annual budget consumed in one event.

Recovery:    rollback immediately, verify, communicate.
Post-mortem: 1. why did canary miss it?
             2. was rollback < 60s (auto) or < 5min (manual)?
             3. were right metrics watched during canary?
Action:      mandatory canary + auto-rollback on error/latency thresholds
             + pre-deploy checks + regular rollback drills
```

### Q5. Your database primary fails. Automated failover to the replica takes 90 seconds, but you targeted 99.99%. Is that acceptable?
**Answer:** Probably yes, with caveats. A single 90-second failover per year consumes 90 seconds of the 52-minute annual budget — about 3% — leaving room for other incidents. The real question is how often primary failures occur. If they happen once a year, 90 seconds per failure is fine. If they happen monthly, you would consume 18 minutes of the budget just on failovers, leaving little for anything else. The second question is what happens during the 90 seconds. If users see 500s, those count against availability. If the system queues writes and retries, availability may be preserved at the cost of latency. The third question is whether 90 seconds is the p50 or the p99 — automated failover can occasionally take much longer if the replica is behind or if the failover logic itself fails. To tighten this: (1) make failover faster — RDS Multi-AZ failover is typically 60–120 seconds; Aurora is 10–30 seconds; (2) use synchronous replication so the replica has all committed writes (no data loss, faster promotion); (3) test failover regularly so the p99 is bounded; (4) ensure clients retry with backoff so brief failovers are masked from users. Ninety seconds is acceptable but not great; aim for under 30 seconds with synchronous replicas and tested automation.

**Visual:**
```
90-second failover @ 1 failure/year  -> 90s of 52-min budget  (3%)  OK
90-second failover @ 12 failures/year -> 18 min of 52-min budget (35%)  NOT OK

During failover:
   500s returned -> counts against availability
   queued + retried -> latency spike, but availability preserved

Tighten: synchronous replica, Aurora-style failover (<30s),
         regular failover drills, client-side retry with backoff.
```

### Q6. You are designing a system where a single region's failure must not lose data, but cross-region sync writes are too slow. What pattern do you use?
**Answer:** This is the classic tension between strong consistency and latency in geo-distributed systems, and the standard resolution is **async replication with a durability guarantee plus a queue-based write path**. The pattern: writes go to a queue (Kafka) in the local region, are durably persisted there, and are then replicated asynchronously to the other region. The local primary consumes the queue and applies the write; the remote primary does the same from the replicated copy. Because the write is durable in the local queue before the client is acked, a region failure does not lose data — the local queue survives long enough for the cross-region replication to catch up, and if the local region is destroyed, the queue contents are still in the remote region's copy (if queue mirroring was on). The trade-off is explicit: the remote region lags by the replication delay (typically 100ms–1s), so a failover to the remote region may serve briefly stale reads, and a write that completed locally but had not yet replicated when the region died will appear as "completed" to the client but not yet visible in the remote region. For most workloads (social posts, messages, logins) this is acceptable; for payments, you would use synchronous cross-region replication and accept the latency. The architectural lesson: geo-distributed systems almost always use async replication with a durability backstop, and the system explicitly reasons about RPO (recovery point objective — how much data loss is tolerable) and RTO (recovery time objective — how fast must service resume).

**Visual:**
```
Region A                                Region B
client -> [Kafka-A] (durable) --async replicate--> [Kafka-B]
            |                                          |
            v                                          v
         [primary-A]                              [primary-B]

Properties:
  - write acked after Kafka-A is durable (low latency)
  - region A dies -> Kafka-B still has the writes -> no data loss
  - region B may lag 100ms-1s -> failover serves briefly stale reads
  - RPO ~= 0, RTO ~= minutes (DNS failover)
```

### Q7. Your team wants to "increase availability" by adding more redundancy. Push back appropriately.
**Answer:** More redundancy is not always better — past a point, it can actually reduce availability. The pushback has four parts. First, **redundancy has diminishing returns**: going from 1 instance to 2 eliminates the single point of failure (a huge availability win); going from 2 to 3 adds marginal benefit; going from 10 to 20 adds almost nothing. The first two or three replicas capture most of the availability gain. Second, **more components means more failure surface**: every additional replica is another thing that can fail, alert, need patching, and drift in configuration. Operational complexity grows super-linearly with component count, and operational mistakes are a leading cause of outages. Third, **redundancy without tested failover is worthless**: ten replicas that have never been failed over to will not save you when the primary dies — the failover mechanism itself is the bottleneck, and adding more replicas does not exercise it. Fourth, **the bottleneck may not be redundancy at all**: if your outages come from bad deploys, dependency failures, or config errors, more replicas will not help — those failure modes affect all replicas simultaneously. The right move is to ask "what failure mode are we trying to survive?" and invest in the specific mitigation for that mode — canary deploys for bad-deploy risk, circuit breakers for dependency risk, multi-region for region risk — rather than reflexively adding replicas.

**Visual:**
```
Availability gain vs replicas:
   ^
   |   steep gain (1->2->3)
   |   ___________  diminishing (3->5->10)
   |                flat (10->20)
   +-------------------------> replicas

Wrong question: "how do we add more redundancy?"
Right question: "what failure mode are we trying to survive?"
   - bad deploy       -> canary + auto-rollback
   - dependency fail  -> circuit breaker + bulkhead
   - region failure   -> multi-region active-active
   - config drift     -> IaC + drift detection
```
